title: Bilinear representation mitigates reversal curse and enables consistent model editing
claim: Relations can be encoded as linear maps or vector translations; a relation-specific bilinear interaction between subject and object is a distinct, richer alternative.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, formulas beneath each, panel (c) in 3D stacked grids
description: Three schematics compare ways to encode a relation between a subject and an object, with an equation and caption under each. Panel (a), on the left, is a flat grid of gray rounded boxes in rows labeled Tracy, Lance, Smith and son, joined by arrows. A blue highlighted block marks the region where the subject s_l feeds diagonally into the object o_L, which is labeled Cory. Its equation is o_L = W_r s_l + b_r. Panels (b) and (c), on the right, show two stacked isometric grids of boxes. The top grid is labeled Tracy Lance Smith and the bottom grid is labeled Cory Lance Smith. Two yellow nodes, s_l and o_l, are linked by dashed blue vertical lines. The equations are o_l = s_l + v_r for (b) and f_r(s_l, o_l) = o_l^T M_r s_l for (c). The eye goes first to the yellow nodes and the blue box.
caption: Schematics of relational embedding structures. For a subject $s$ and object $o$, the relation $r$ is modeled as: (a) linear transformation, (b) vector translation, or (c) bilinear interaction mediated by a relation-specific matrix $M_r$. As an example, in the fact "Son of Tracy Lance Smith is Cory Lance Smith," $s$ is "Tracy Lance Smith,” $o$ is "Cory Lance Smith," and $r$ is son.
abstract: The reversal curse--a language model's inability to infer an unseen fact "B is A" from a learned fact "A is B"--is widely considered a fundamental limitation. We show that this is not an inherent failure but an artifact of how models encode knowledge. Our results demonstrate that training from scratch on synthetic relational knowledge graphs leads to the emergence of a bilinear relational structure within the models' hidden representations. This structure alleviates the reversal curse and facilitates inference of unseen reverse facts. Crucially, this bilinear geometry is foundational for consistent model editing: updates to a single fact propagate correctly to its reverse and logically dependent relations. In contrast, models lacking this representation suffer from the reversal curse and fail to generalize model edits, leading to logical inconsistencies. Our results establish that training on a relational knowledge dataset induces the emergence of bilinear internal representations, which in turn support language models in behaving in a logically consistent manner after editing. This suggests that the efficacy of language model editing depends not only on the choice of algorithm but on the underlying representational geometry of the knowledge itself.
